records.water_estimate_basis: Admissible sources describe drought tolerance qualitatively rather than as a checkable schedule. MOBOT's structured field rates "Water: Medium"; UF/IFAS's structured field rates "Drought tolerance: high"; Clemson's Quick Guide lists "Watering: Drought-tolerant once established"; NC State's description states the tree "is tolerant of drought, heat and air pollution." No admissible source gives a numeric watering-frequency interval or a soil-check depth for this species, and the qualitative ratings vary from "Medium" to "high," so no single water_regime category was forced.
unknowns: day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives ambient day/night temperature ranges, humidity requirements, or foot-candle light measurements for this outdoor landscape tree; these read as indoor-microclimate fields that don't apply to a 50-80 ft shade tree.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)" defines the minimum threshold for its 'Full Sun' category, not a species-specific maximum, so it was not mapped to this field.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a specific cold-damage-onset temperature. Only USDA hardiness-zone survival data exists (NC State: 3a-9b; Clemson: 4-8b; UF/IFAS: 3A-8A; MOBOT: Zone 3-8; RHS: H6, hardy to -20 to -15C), which describes winter survivability across a very wide range, not an actionable damage threshold. This is expected for one of the hardiest, most cold-tolerant landscape trees available, not under-research.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source describes a distinct dormancy/cool-rest care regimen beyond Ginkgo being a normal winter-deciduous tree.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: RHS's 'Potentially harmful' field states "Seed TOXIC to pets - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers" -- this is the only admissible-source language naming 'pets' at all, but it never names cats or dogs specifically, so per this catalog's convention it does not meet the bar for toxic_to_pets=true and the field is left null. NC State's detailed structured poison data (Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Irritation of the skin following contact with the juice of the seed pulp; irritation of lips, mouth, and throat and stomach pain, nausea, and diarrhea after eating the pulp."; Poison Toxic Principle: "An alkyl phenol and ginkgolic acid"; Poison Part: Seeds) is explicitly filed under a 'Poisonous to Humans' section header, not a pet-toxicity section, so it was not blended into toxicity_detail either. UGA's 'Poisonous Plants in the Landscape' circular (C-957) lists "Ginkgo (female) | Ginkgo biloba | fruit | violent stomach pain, kidney disorders" in a table whose introduction frames the whole document around 'young children or pets' broadly, but the per-species table entry itself does not name cats, dogs, or any specific animal for Ginkgo, so it also does not support toxic_to_pets. Clemson notes "Skin irritation from ginkgolic acid in the pulp" without naming any animal.

Species note (dioecious trees, no dedicated field in this schema): Ginkgo biloba is dioecious, with separate male and female trees, and this materially affects what a home gardener should select. NC State: "they are dioecious with separate male and female trees" and "Seeds from female trees are messy and have foul-smelling flesh, so planting grafted male trees is often preferable... Most of the ornamental ginkgoes in the United States are male." MOBOT: "Ginkgos are dioecious (separate male and female trees). Nurseries typically sell only male trees because female trees produce seeds encased in fleshy, fruit-like cone which, at maturity in autumn, are messy and emit a noxious, foul odor upon falling to the ground and splitting open." Clemson: "Ginkgos are dioecious (derived from the Greek meaning 'two houses'), with male and female reproductive parts on separate trees" and recommends gardeners "choose male cultivars to avoid messy, foul-smelling fruit." RHS: "Unpleasantly scented dull yellow fruits in autumn on female plants." UF/IFAS: "Only male plants should be used as the female produces foul smelling fruit in late autumn" and fruit "emits a pungent odor some find to be offensive." Penn State Extension ("Strange Fruit"): "The tree has separate male and female trees; only the female trees bear 'fruit'... as the fruit matures and drops from the tree, it develops a fetid 'what did I step in' shoe-checking, retch-inducing odor." This is decision-relevant for a home gardener (buy a named male cultivar to avoid the mess/odor) but has no dedicated field in this schema, so it is captured here rather than dropped.

Seed/fruit-pulp toxicity to humans (distinct from human dietary-supplement leaf-extract literature, which is a different context and out of scope, and which no admissible source addresses anyway): NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' section rates Poison Severity "Low" and describes symptoms as "TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Irritation of the skin following contact with the juice of the seed pulp; irritation of lips, mouth, and throat and stomach pain, nausea, and diarrhea after eating the pulp," with toxic principle "An alkyl phenol and ginkgolic acid," Poison Part "Seeds," and "Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes." Clemson separately flags "Skin irritation from ginkgolic acid in the pulp" as a common problem. RHS: "Seeds harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." UGA's poisonous-plants circular lists the fruit as causing "violent stomach pain, kidney disorders." This body of evidence addresses the fleshy seed-coat/pulp as a contact irritant and, on ingestion in quantity, the seed kernel itself -- kept separate from any leaf-extract dietary-supplement toxicity discussion per the research brief.

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: NC State's structured Soil pH field checks all three of its fixed site-wide categories together -- "Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0)" -- meaning broad tolerance, but the numeric bounds in parentheses are NC State's standard category definitions reused across its whole Plant Toolbox, not a range picked specifically for Ginkgo, and the open-ended "<6.0"/">8.0" wording gives no closed numeric bound to record. No other admissible source states a numeric pH range for this species (Clemson, RHS, UF/IFAS, and MOBOT all describe soil pH only categorically -- acidic/alkaline tolerance, "Well-drained" moisture -- without numbers), so both fields are left null.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: UF/IFAS's only fertilizing guidance is "particularly if it receives an adequate supply of water and some fertilizer" -- no interval, calendar month, or dilution strength is given by any admissible source.

is_houseplant / bonsai and container use: NC State's description notes "Its sculptural form makes it popular for use in bonsai," and other NC State cultivar pages show the dwarf 'Mariken' cultivar potted, but bonsai/potted display is not the same as sustained indoor houseplant culture -- ginkgo is winter-deciduous and needs an outdoor winter chill/dormancy period, and no admissible source frames it as grown indoors long-term. Every admissible source instead uniformly describes it as a 50-80+ ft outdoor landscape/street/shade tree, so is_houseplant is kept false.

water_regime: left null. This is an in-ground landscape tree, and the container-oriented enum (keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist) doesn't fit any admissible source's framing. Sources vary in how they characterize water need -- MOBOT's structured field rates "Water: Medium," UF/IFAS rates "Drought tolerance: high," Clemson's Quick Guide lists "Watering: Drought-tolerant once established," and NC State's description says the tree "is tolerant of drought." This qualitative drought-tolerance picture is captured in water_estimate_basis instead of forcing it into the container-watering enum.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est: no admissible source frames watering for this species as a checkable schedule (soil-probe depth, days-between-waterings); guidance is only qualitative drought-tolerance language.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note is non-null but, unlike every other narrative field in this record (e.g. water_estimate_basis, whose four citations are all explicitly labeled 'water_estimate_basis (...)'), no citation in the array has a claim label that literally contains the string 'name_note.' Per structural check 1 this field fails the mechanical citation-tracing test. That said, the underlying content checks out: I fetched the live RHS page and confirmed the 'Name Status' field does read 'Correct' verbatim, and fetched NC State's page and confirmed the Genus/Species/Family field reads 'Ginkgo' / 'biloba' / 'Ginkgoaceae' verbatim -- both facts are already captured under citations 2 (scientific_name_given) and 3 (scientific_name_accepted). So this is a citation-labeling/traceability gap specific to the name_note field, not a factual error -- the record simply never added a name_note-labeled citation the way it did for water_estimate_basis.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's poison profile (Poison Severity: High; Poison Toxic Principle: cyanogenic glycosides; Poison Part: fruits, leaves, stems) states that hydrogen cyanide is highly poisonous if ingested in quantity and that all parts are toxic to humans, cats, dogs, livestock, and horses, with weakness, incoordination, seizures, coma, respiratory failure, and death possible from ingestion. RHS separately confirms pet toxicity for this species, naming dogs specifically ("Pets (dogs, poultry): Harmful if eaten"). Note: bird/wildlife toxicity (notably cedar waxwing mortality from the cyanogenic berries) is a distinct, separately well-documented finding -- see unknowns; it is not folded into this pets-scoped detail.
unknowns: day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: no admissible source gives target ambient day or night temperatures for this outdoor landscape shrub.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source frames a dormancy or cool-rest period for this species.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source; this species is documented only as an outdoor landscape shrub, never as a plant grown under measured indoor humidity.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' defines the entry threshold for its Full Sun light category, not a stated maximum for this species, so it was not mapped onto this field.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: NC State lists all three of its pH categories for this species (Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, Alkaline >8.0) with no stated floor or ceiling, and RHS independently gives pH tolerance as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- together these describe essentially unrestricted pH tolerance rather than a bounded range, so no defensible min or max could be set.

Established plants have some drought tolerance.') that doesn't map cleanly onto the schema's container-oriented dry-down regime categories; no admissible source gives a numeric watering interval or soil-check depth for this outdoor shrub.

is_houseplant is set to false on hardiness-zone/outdoor-landscape evidence (NC State USDA zones 6a-9b; Missouri Botanical Garden zone 6 to 9); no admissible source describes growing Nandina domestica indoors or in containers long-term.

chill_damage_f 10 is drawn from Missouri Botanical Garden's note that in their own reference garden ('In the St. Louis area') the species drops its foliage and sometimes suffers stem dieback once winter temperatures fall below 10°F -- the only damage-onset figure any admissible source gives, though it is framed around MOBOT's own local growing conditions rather than asserted as a universal species-wide constant. No other admissible source offers a competing or corroborating damage-onset number, so it was used as-is with this caveat noted.

Toxicity to birds/wildlife is a separate, well-documented finding distinct from pet toxicity: Clemson HGIC ('The berries contain the toxin cyanide, which causes bird mortality. Cedar waxwings are most susceptible...'), NC State ('birds such as the Cedar Waxwing'), and Missouri Botanical Garden ('the berries of Nandina domestica have been linked to toxicity in cedar waxwing birds') all independently confirm this. This catalog's toxic_to_pets field tracks only cats/dogs, and the schema has no separate wildlife-toxicity field, so this finding is documented here rather than folded into toxic_to_pets or toxicity_detail.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: NC State's poison data sits under a 'Poisonous to Humans:' section label, but the quoted 'Poison Symptoms' sentence itself explicitly names cats and dogs as toxic targets, and the page's separate 'Problems' tag list carries 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Dogs' as their own sibling entries rather than being nested inside a humans-only subsection -- so despite the section header, this source affirmatively supports pet toxicity and was used accordingly. This was cross-checked against Clemson HGIC, whose toxicity section is scoped only to wildlife/birds and never names cats, dogs, or any pet -- so Clemson was used for the bird-toxicity note above but NOT as support for toxic_to_pets.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note asserts that 'NC State Extension, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden, and UF/IFAS all consistently use "Nandina domestica"' -- but the record's citations array contains zero entries from either admissible UF/IFAS domain (edis.ifas.ufl.edu or ask.ifas.ufl.edu). I confirmed live that UF/IFAS does have EDIS content touching Nandina domestica (e.g. ENH1158/EP418 on 'Harbour Dwarf' Nandina, and fact sheet FP422), so a citation may have been obtainable, but none was produced -- the claim was asserted, not sourced.

soil_ph_min: NC State's structured pH field lists 'Acid (<6.0)' as a checked category with no numeric lower bound given, so only soil_ph_max (8.0, from the 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' category) could be set.

fertilize_active_months: Clemson specifies 'early spring and midsummer' rather than named calendar months, so these were not converted into month numbers as the rules only permit translating an explicitly named month.

Clemson's fertilizing schedule and houseplant/greenhouse guidance, and the RHS growing-guide's night-temperature and overwintering guidance, come from each publisher's genus-level 'Bougainvillea' page rather than a glabra-specific page. Used because B. glabra is the principal species these generalist factsheets describe and no species-specific admissible source conflicts with them; for is_houseplant and soil_base, the RHS glabra-specific species page independently corroborates the same container/loam-compost guidance.

soil_drainage (fast): drawn from NC State's 'Good Drainage' / 'Occasionally Dry' checkboxes on the glabra-specific page. The same NC State soil-type field also lists 'Clay' and 'High Organic Matter' as tolerated soil types, which sits in some tension with fast drainage, and RHS separately describes container soil as 'Moist but well-drained' rather than fast-draining. Not a harm-capable field per the rules, so not nulled, but flagged here as an internal-source tension worth noting.

soil_base — removed on audit: soil_base's only citation is the same RHS text verified above: 'Plant in large pots of peat-free, loam-based compost, or directly into the conservatory border.' 'Loam-based compost' (a specific, formulated potting medium, akin to John Innes-type mixes) is not the same thing as a generic 'standard_potting' category, and no other citation in the record supports soil_base at all. The claim label asserts a category ('standard_potting') the quote does not literally support, with no independent corroboration.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: Verified the full source sentence on hgic.clemson.edu: 'Outdoors, bougainvilleas should be in full sun... They should be fertilized at half the recommended rate once a month with a general-purpose fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10) in early spring and midsummer.' This single sentence is genuinely ambiguous about whether 'once a month' is a standing, year-round 30-day cadence or refers only to monthly feeding confined to the two named windows (i.e., could mean as few as two applications total, not a recurring interval). The record itself judged this same sentence's timing language too ambiguous to convert into fertilize_active_months (left null, with an explicit note that only named calendar months would be converted), yet extracted a precise '30' for fertilize_interval_days from that identical ambiguous clause -- an inconsistent reading of one uncertain source sentence, and the numeric field's value is not cleanly derivable from a quote this self-contradictory.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The citation's quote for this field is selectively truncated. I fetched the live NC State page: the actual 'Poison Symptoms' text reads '...Severe nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, and episodes of irregular heartbeat. Consumption of leaves in "herbal medicine" is not recommended.' before continuing to 'Toxic Principle: cyanogenic glycosides.' The record's quote stops right after 'irregular heartbeat' and splices directly to 'Toxic Principle,' silently dropping the herbal-medicine sentence. That dropped sentence is the tell that NC State's Poison Severity/Poison Symptoms/Toxic Principle/Poison Part block is a single undifferentiated field describing consumption risk in general (tied to human herbal use of the leaves), not a symptom set broken out per affected animal -- the same block sits underneath tags for 'Poisonous to Humans,' 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' 'Problem for Horses,' and 'Problem for Children' with no species-specific differentiation anywhere on the page. Presenting this exact symptom list as pet-specific toxicity_detail overstates what the source establishes. (Note: toxic_to_pets itself is fine -- the same source's tags explicitly name both 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Dogs' as categorical flags, independent of the disputed symptom narrative.)

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The only supporting citation's quote is 'Design Feature: Border, Mass Planting, Screen/Privacy' -- a landscape-use tag that says nothing about indoor or container culture. The claim label's parenthetical 'no indoor or container culture described' is the researcher's own inference from absence of evidence, not something the quote states; NC State's toolbox does not have a houseplant field being checked here at all. There is no independent citation that actually asserts a houseplant/non-houseplant status for this species, so the boolean is only circumstantially supported, not directly evidenced.

chill_damage_f: no source gives a Fahrenheit damage-onset figure. RHS gives only a categorical Hardiness rating (H5: 'hardy in most places throughout the UK even in severe winters (-15 to -10)', in Celsius) and NC State/Missouri Botanical Garden give only USDA Zones 4-8 -- these are survival/hardiness-zone statements, not a specific damage-onset temperature, so were not mapped onto this field.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed as an actionable care target by any admissible source. Clemson's Vine Selections factsheet notes the species is 'Intolerant of heat and humidity,' but that is a regional climate-suitability warning (i.e., it struggles in hot, humid summers), not a stated humidity percentage or care-level category, so it was not mapped to this field.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good: not stated by any source -- all give categorical outdoor shade/light descriptions (Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade, Partial Shade, part shade to full shade), not indoor footcandle levels; this species is not documented as grown under measured indoor light.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's own 'Partial Shade' category is defined with a 2-6 hour range, but this is a generic category-boundary definition applied site-wide on NC State's toolbox, not a stated species-specific maximum sun-hours figure for climbing hydrangea itself.

outdoor_sun_exposure -- full_sun intentionally excluded: sources conflict. NC State's species-specific structured Light field offers only Dappled Sunlight/Deep shade/Partial Shade, with no full-sun option at all. Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Sun field says only 'Part shade to full shade,' and its Culture text conditions any full-sun tolerance on 'consistently moist soils' while separately warning the plant is 'somewhat intolerant of the hot and humid conditions of the deep South.' UMD's vine table likewise lists only 'Partial shade to full shade.' Against that, RHS's Position tag unconditionally lists 'Full sun, Partial shade,' but RHS's own Cultivation prose on the same page conditions it ('grow in sun if soil remains reliably moist'), and Clemson's Vine Selections factsheet table separately lists 'Full sun to part shade' for this species while also flagging it as 'Intolerant of heat and humidity.' Given this genuine mix of unconditional, conditional, and absent full-sun support -- and the plant-harm relevance of overstating full-sun tolerance for a species multiple sources flag as heat/humidity sensitive -- full_sun was left out of the array rather than asserted as an unconditional value; part_shade and full_shade are cleanly and consistently supported across all five admissible sources.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: NC State gives only broad categories (Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, Alkaline >8.0) spanning nearly the entire pH scale, and RHS gives only 'Acid or Neutral' with no numeric figures; no admissible source states a specific numeric min/max pH for this species, so no defensible bound could be set.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives fertilizer timing, interval, or strength guidance for this species. A Penn State Extension URL once titled 'the-climbing-hydrangea' now 301-redirects to a generic ornamentals-species-listing page with no species-specific fertilizing content, so it could not be used as a source.

water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a specific watering-interval number of days, a soil moisture-check depth, or a dry-down target for this species; sources describe qualitative soil-moisture preference only ('moist but well-drained,' 'fertile, moist, well-drained soil,' 'moist, well-draining'), which supports the categorical water_regime value but not a numeric estimate.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The value is literally the JSON string "null" (quoted) rather than a real JSON null -- confirmed by inspecting the record text character-for-character. This is a direct violation of structural check 6, and it also fails structural check 1 independently: since the value is technically a populated string, not null, it would need a citation whose claim label contains 'scientific_name_accepted', but no such citation exists (only 'name_note ...' citations touch this content). Cross-checking the rest of this catalog (e.g. app/data/verified/b14-annual-flowers2.json line 206: "scientific_name_accepted": null) confirms the house convention for a genuinely unresolved accepted name is real JSON null, so this is a deviation, not a stylistic choice. Note the underlying research is sound -- I independently fetched RHS (Name Status 'Correct' for Hydrangea petiolaris, listing 'Hydrangea anomala subsp. petiolaris' as a synonym), NC State (Scientific Name 'Hydrangea petiolaris', 'Previously known as: Hydrangea anomala ssp. petiolaris'), and Missouri Botanical Garden ('Subsp. petiolaris (formerly known as Hydrangea petiolaris)') and all three quotes are verbatim-accurate, so the two-against-one conflict is genuine and the intent to leave it unresolved is correct -- only the encoding is broken. Downstream code that checks `if value is not None` would treat this as a populated field and could literally display the text "null" to a user.

None of the three literally uses 'cactus' or 'succulent' for the medium, so 'cactus_succulent' was not forced despite the plant's succulent habit; 'standard_potting' is also a poor fit given all three sources specifically emphasize added grit/fast drainage over an unamended standard mix. direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's light field reads 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' -- the site's fixed definition of its 'Full sun' category, reused verbatim across unrelated species pages, not a figure curated for this species -- so it supported only the outdoor_sun_exposure category, not a numeric hours value.
